1) High-latency traces: get_traces returned multiple traces >=8s (examples: traceIDs 3e30f8047d13a46aa608701184fe9b82 latency 13s, 8e0b3420ad58f38db5ba64f9cd80d4bc 11s, etc.).

The Envoy spans include upstream_cluster="frontend" and upstream_address="10.96.18.88:8080", and response_flags='-' (no upstream timeout error) — showing the proxy itself spent several seconds waiting/processing upstream traffic and contributed the largest single-span delay.
3) Proxy logs: frontend-proxy logs show a runtime warning: "There is no configured limit to the number of allowed active downstream connections." Conclusion: the evidence (large Envoy spans in multiple high-latency traces, with downstream services being faster) indicates frontend-proxy is the observable epicenter of the frontend-origin latency.

insights: Multiple recent high-latency traces involve the frontend-proxy service (several >= 8s; examples: traceIDs 3e30f8047d13a46aa608701184fe9b82 ~13s, 8e0b3420ad58f38db5ba64f9cd80d4bc ~11s, 09056a998645b95e97a5a9a66fee10ea ~21s) — indicating a recurring proxy-related latency pattern.

Detailed trace (3e30f8047d13a46aa608701184fe9b82) shows Envoy/frontend-proxy spans with large durations (~5957ms and ~6124ms) that account for the bulk of the end-to-end latency, while downstream service spans (frontend, product-catalog, DB) are shorter (frontend ~4.4s/4.0s in-process spans; product-catalog ~3.4s; DB ~622ms).

Envoy span metadata shows upstream_cluster="frontend" and upstream_address="10.96.18.88:8080" with response_flags='-' (no explicit upstream timeout or upstream error), meaning the proxy itself spent significant time waiting/processing rather than failing fast due to an upstream error.

Frontend-proxy logs contain a runtime warning: "There is no configured limit to the number of allowed active downstream connections." This is a misconfiguration/resource-control clue that can lead to excessive connection handling, buffering, or stalls under load.

No explicit upstream timeout/retry error messages were present in the sampled proxy logs; the traces (large proxy spans) combined with the log warning point to proxy-level resource/handling (connection/concurrency or buffering) issues rather than backend service errors.

Correlation of traces and logs supports the conclusion that the frontend-proxy (Envoy) is the observable epicenter of the latency (confirmed hypothesis). The hypothesis that downstream services were the primary cause is not supported by the trace timings.

Likely root-cause class: proxy-level resource/handling misconfiguration or saturation (e.g., missing connection limits, connection handling/backpressure, or Envoy buffering behavior) causing multi-second stalls in Envoy spans. Recommended follow-ups (implied by findings): configure resource limits (global_downstream_max_connections), inspect Envoy listener/cluster timeouts and connection pool settings, review proxy resource usage and concurrency under load, and reproduce with detailed Envoy admin/stats if needed.

final_report.root_cause: Envoy proxy (frontend-proxy) manifesting proxy-level stalls due to an unbounded downstream connection configuration (runtime warning: "There is no configured limit to the number of allowed active downstream connections"). Under observed load the proxy spent multiple seconds inside Envoy/router spans (many ~6s–10s Envoy spans and end-to-end traces ~10s), indicating connection/handling or buffering saturation inside the proxy rather than slow backend processing. This caused frontend requests (including calls to image-provider) to be blocked/held in Envoy for multi-second intervals and produced the high-latency symptoms.

final_report.investigation_summary: Priority-1 investigation (completed): Inspected high-latency traces and frontend-proxy logs. No upstream timeout flags were present in the Envoy spans (response_flags='-'), i.e., Envoy spent time waiting/processing rather than failing fast. Conclusion: frontend-proxy (Envoy) is the localized root cause due to proxy-level resource/handling misconfiguration (unbounded downstream connections), which under current load produced multi-second stall behavior and ~10s client-visible request latency.
